body: With the above patch, I see this output: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/mbautin/e4ca34ddd210de350f13d6726a3b2181/raw

For more than 10.5 ms, we are stuck in a state of 3 microseconds remaining to the deadline, so the deadline is not considered expired.

```
I0106 17:50:34.371387 214437 backoff_waiter.h:47] ExpiredAt: time=8254829278 us; deadline_=8254829281 us; time to deadline=3 us; expired: 0
. . .
I0106 17:50:34.381896 214437 backoff_waiter.h:47] ExpiredAt: time=8254829278 us; deadline_=8254829281 us; time to deadline=3 us; expired: 0
```

Using the approach described at https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58189790/do-clock-monotonic-and-clock-monotonic-coarse-have-the-same-base, I get the resolution of 10 ms for the coarse monotonic clock on AWS Graviton 2 CentOS 8 machine (10^7 nanoseconds):
```
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE resolution is: 0 sec, 10000000 nsec
```

rename.to: CoarseBackoffWaiter can get into a busy loop, ClientUnitTest.TestRetryFunc fails on aarch64

body: CoarseBackoffWaiter is being used in transaction status resolution (`TransactionStatusCache::DoGetCommitData()`), and if we get into busy wait loops there, that might explain the drop in performance on aarch64 with higher load.
It also remains to be explained why the issue with coarse monotonic clock granularity does not occur on x86_64. Does the coarse monotonic clock have a much finer granularity on x86_64?

@spolitov mentioned to me that he thinks we can just add the clock resolution to the delay in case we haven't reached the deadline but the remaining time is extremely small. Or, I guess, we could round the delay up to the clock resolution.

> It also remains to be explained why the issue with coarse monotonic clock granularity does not occur on x86_64. Does the coarse monotonic clock have a much finer granularity on x86_64?

This does appear to be the case, on a n1-standard-4 centos instance the coarse monotonic clock granularity was 1ms (incidentally, on an ubuntu x86_64 laptop it was 4ms, and the test generally passes but does occasionally fail). But even though just ensuring the delay is at least the coarse monotonic clock granularity seems to fix the problem, it doesn't appear to be the actual issue, since multiplying everything by 10 (base delay, jitter, test duration) still results in the same issue.

Rather, I think the real issue is that it appears that time observed on x86_64 has intervals of the clock granularity _plus_ some delta (~10-100s of ns), whereas time observed on aarch64 has intervals of the clock granularity _minus_ some delta (~10-100s of ns). This means that when we attempt to wait for 1s (the duration set for the test), we actually wait for 1s + x (~us) on x86_64 (this is ok, test passes!) and for 1s - x (~us) on aarch64 (this is not ok! we end up with a tiny bit of time left (~us), but trying to sleep for that duration results in no observable sleep at all, since it rounds down to 0). Occasionally, by chance, we actually end up waiting for 1.01s (things ended up rounding up with the last wait), and this causes the test to sporadically pass on aarch64, but otherwise, it fails.

This can actually be observed pretty easily just by changing the deadline in the test from now + 1s to now + 999ms: the test now consistently passes because the nearest multiple of the clock granularity is 1000ms, and 1000ms - x (~us) is still larger than 999ms.

But I think given this, the correct fix might be to consider the case where time remaining is under the clock granularity as the deadline being reached (total time of 1s + x/1s - x).

@es1024 thanks for finding the root cause! I think we have two options: always round the delay up to the nearest clock granularity, or, maybe, waiting in increments of e.g. 1ms if adding 10ms to the wait time is too much in some cases (e.g. if the timeout itself is on that order of magnitude). Or we could make this conditional based on the total timeout duration.

Waiting in 1ms increments won't work, since the problem is that the clock can only observe time in 10ms increments (it'd end up just waiting for up to ~10 iterations of 1ms on top of the expected number from exponential backoff, until it hits the next 10ms increment and the clock time changes again); in cases where we need wait times on that order of magnitude, we have to use finer resolution clocks instead. 

Given that the very first wait is set to be anywhere from 4~54ms right now though, timeouts of that magnitude should probably also have the jitter calculation adjusted to be much smaller.
